questions.q: When does the current platform's contract or support end, and what happens if you are still on it then?
questions.why: The date sets the pace of everything else.
questions.need: The deadline is known, and the plan finishes before it with margin
questions.how: Put the end date and the cost of overrunning it in the plan
questions.listen: A renewal or end of support inside twelve months sets the deadline: plan backwards from it with them.
questions.probe: If the move is not finished by then, would you renew for one year or for three, and at what price?

questions.q: What would a failed migration weekend cost, and who would feel it first?
questions.why: Turns risk into a number the business can weigh.
questions.need: The cost of a failed cutover is known, and the plan is shaped around it
questions.how: Agree with the business which applications cannot be down, and for how long
questions.listen: If they can name who suffers, they know the stakes: the plan must protect that service first.
questions.probe: Has a past migration or upgrade gone wrong, and what did it cost?

questions.q: How many virtual machines are there, at which sites, and how many have no clear owner?
questions.why: Machines without owners cannot be scheduled or tested.
questions.need: Every virtual machine is known, with an owner
questions.how: Run discovery at every site and assign owners
questions.listen: Machines with no owner should be retired or parked, not moved: a smaller move is a faster one.
questions.probe: How many of these could be switched off before the move without anyone noticing?

questions.q: Do you know what each application depends on: databases, file shares, licences, hard-coded addresses?
questions.why: Hidden dependencies are what break a cutover.
questions.need: Every application's dependencies are mapped and confirmed by its owner
questions.how: Map dependencies from traffic, then review them with each owner
questions.listen: Hard-coded addresses, licence servers tied to hardware and shared databases with no owner are what break a cutover quietly.
questions.probe: Which application broke the last time an address or a server name changed?

questions.q: Have you migrated anything yet, even in test, and what went wrong?
questions.why: A first test finds the problems cheaply.
questions.need: A test migration of a representative group has run and its findings are closed
questions.how: Migrate one representative group in a test window
questions.listen: Even one test move teaches drivers, tools and timings. None means the first wave should be small and early.
questions.probe: How long did the copy take, and how long was the machine down?

questions.q: If a cutover fails at 3 a.m., how do you go back, and has anyone tried it?
questions.why: Rollback is the safety net for every wave.
questions.need: Every wave has a rollback that has been tested
questions.how: Write and rehearse the rollback for the first wave
questions.listen: A rollback never tried is not a rollback: agree to test one in the pilot.
questions.probe: How long can the old machine be kept, untouched, after its move?

questions.q: Will backup, monitoring and security tools work on the new platform on day one?
questions.why: The platform moves; the tools around it must too.
questions.need: Backup, monitoring and security run on the new platform before the first production wave
questions.how: List every tool that touches the platform and test each on the new one
questions.listen: Tools that call the old platform's management interface break quietly: list them and check each before the first wave.
questions.probe: Which of these tools are up for contract renewal in the same year?

questions.q: Who decides that a wave is done and the old machines can be switched off?
questions.why: Without an owner, the old platform never goes away.
questions.need: Each wave has an owner who signs it off, and the old machines are switched off on schedule
questions.how: Name a wave owner and agree what done means
questions.listen: Without a named owner per wave, old machines stay on and the bill is paid twice.
questions.probe: What check must pass before an old machine can be deleted?

questions.q: Which servers and storage arrays must stay in use, and until when are they supported?
questions.why: Reusing hardware already owned can change the cost and the timing of the move.
questions.need: The hardware that stays is known, with its support dates and whether the new platform can use it
questions.how: List servers and arrays with their end-of-support dates, and check each against the new platform's support list
questions.listen: Reusing hardware still under support lowers the cost of the move: check it against the target's compatibility list.
questions.probe: Which of them appear on the compatibility list of the platforms you are considering?

questions.q: How long can each application be down at cutover, and can its data be copied ahead of time?
questions.why: Copying data ahead and cutting over within days keeps the downtime to the last changes; waiting too long makes the copy grow on the source.
questions.need: Each wave copies its data ahead and cuts over within days, inside a window agreed with the application owner
questions.how: Seed each wave's data ahead and plan its cutover within a week
questions.listen: Minutes, not hours, call for copying data ahead and switching at the end. Systems that can never stop need a plan of their own.
questions.probe: Which systems can never stop, and how are they patched today?

questions.q: Which database servers should be rebuilt on the new platform rather than copied as they are?
questions.why: Moving a database like for like is fast; rebuilding it is the moment to fix versions, layout and licences.
questions.need: Every database server has a decision: move as it is, or rebuild on purpose
questions.how: Review each database server with its DBA and decide move or rebuild
questions.listen: A move is the cheapest moment to upgrade or consolidate databases; copying them as they are carries old problems along.
questions.probe: Which database versions are out of support, and would their owners rather rebuild?

questions.q: What will be visibly better for users and the business after the move, beyond a different platform?
questions.why: A move that changes nothing visible is judged only by its cost and its disruption.
questions.need: Each wave brings an improvement the business can see, named before it starts
questions.how: Agree one visible improvement per wave with its application owner
questions.listen: If the only answer is a cheaper licence, it is a cost exercise: find the one thing users will feel.
questions.probe: What would you show the board six months after the move?

questions.q: Who checks each application after its move, and against which baseline?
questions.why: Without a baseline, "it feels slower" cannot be answered, and sign-off drifts.
questions.need: Every application has an owner who tests it against a baseline taken before the move, then signs off or rolls back
questions.how: Take performance baselines before the first wave and name who signs off each application
questions.listen: A baseline taken before the move settles arguments about performance after it.
questions.probe: Which measurement would convince the application owner that nothing got worse?

questions.q: Will machines get their labels as they move, so protection and security apply on arrival?
questions.why: Labelling after the move leaves a window in which machines run unprotected.
questions.need: Machines are labelled as they move, and protection and security policies apply on arrival
questions.how: Map labels to policies before the first wave and put labelling in the runbook
questions.listen: Labelling during the move means protection and security rules apply on arrival, not retrofitted later.
questions.probe: Who owns the naming and labelling rules today?

questions.q: What comes after the move: which services should the platform offer in one, two and three years?
questions.why: The plan after the migration is where the platform pays back; without one, the move stops at a replacement.
questions.need: A dated plan for the services after the migration is agreed, with an owner
questions.how: Write the next services (self-service, databases, containers, recovery) into a dated roadmap
questions.listen: A roadmap past the move (databases, containers, AI, self-service) turns a replacement into a platform choice.
questions.probe: Which request from the business could the new platform answer that the old one never did?

questions.q: Are containers or Kubernetes clusters running on the current platform, and who runs them?
questions.why: Container platforms built on the old hypervisor are easy to miss and hard to move.
questions.need: Container workloads on the current platform are listed with an owner
questions.how: List clusters running on the current platform and where their data lives
questions.listen: Clusters tied to the old platform's add-ons need a target of their own; found late, they delay the last wave.
questions.probe: Which of them keep data in volumes provided by the old platform?

questions.q: Which machines rely on special devices or settings: passed-through hardware, raw or shared disks, very large memory?
questions.why: Unusual configurations are where conversion tools stop.
questions.need: Machines with special devices or shared disks are listed, each with a plan
questions.how: Filter the inventory for passed-through devices, raw and shared disks
questions.listen: Each needs a decision: convert, rebuild or leave. A handful is normal; dozens need a wave of their own.
questions.probe: Which clusters use shared disks, and could they use another way of clustering?

questions.q: How much data changes per day on the largest systems, and how much bandwidth is there between old and new?
questions.why: Daily change and bandwidth decide how long the first copy and the final sync take.
questions.need: Daily change and bandwidth are measured for the largest systems
questions.how: Measure daily change on the ten largest machines and the link between them
questions.listen: If the first copy of the biggest systems takes days, start it early and keep it in sync until cutover.
questions.probe: Is the link shared with production traffic, and can the copy be slowed during the day?

questions.q: Which operating systems are in scope, and how many are out of their vendor's support?
questions.why: Old systems may lack the drivers or the support a new platform needs.
questions.need: Operating systems are listed with their support status
questions.how: Group the inventory by operating system and version
questions.listen: Unsupported systems are a risk wherever they run: the move is the moment to decide on each.
questions.probe: Which applications keep those old systems alive, and who owns them?

questions.q: Who will run the new platform, and what training or help do they need before the first production wave?
questions.why: A team that is not ready slows every wave after the first.
questions.need: The operating team is named and trained before the production waves
questions.how: Agree a training plan and a pilot run by the team itself
questions.listen: If the same small team must run the old platform, the move and the new one, the plan must leave them time.
questions.probe: Who will be on call for the new platform in its first month?
